entities.description:
The residual sum of squares divided by n is MSDₙ. Divide the decomposition by n, then subtract Δ².
The result holds for every sample, not only on average. Estimating the center removes the nonnegative squared shift between the centers.
For a real realized sample, μ and therefore δ = x̄−μ are generally unknown. The identity is explanatory, not a recipe requiring knowledge of μ.
entities.label: bf ex1

entities.description:
Bias concerns the estimator's average over hypothetical repetitions, not one observed value.
Use U = the squared-distance average about μ, V = Δ² and c = −1 in the previously introduced linearity rule.
Finite population variance makes the required moments finite. This linearity step does not itself require independence.
entities.label: bf ex2

entities.description:
The count n is fixed across repetitions. Move 1/n outside E and distribute E over the finite sum.
Each remaining expectation concerns an individual squared deviation about the fixed population mean.
Independence is unnecessary for this use of linearity; it will matter when computing the variance of the sample mean.
entities.label: bf ex3

entities.description:
Each observation has population expectation μ and variance σ². The variance definition gives E[(Xᵢ−μ)²] = σ² for every i.
Substitute σ² into the finite average. Summing the same σ² n times and dividing by n returns σ².
This determines the theoretical first term even though the numerical value of σ² is usually unknown. The model supplies its symbolic value, not its measured value.
entities.label: bf ex4

entities.description:
The intervening sample-mean derivation established E[Δ²] = σ²/n under iid finite-variance sampling.
Replace that theoretical expectation in the MSD equation. We have not calculated Δ from the concrete sample.
This is why a mathematical model can quantify the average shortfall without revealing the unknown population mean or variance numerically.
entities.label: bf ex5

entities.description:
In the general factorization use a = σ².
The fraction left after subtraction is (n−1)/n, strictly less than one for n > 1. Thus the MSD is biased downward when σ² > 0.
A particular realized MSD may lie above or below σ². Bias is the repeated-sampling expectation, not the direction of every individual error.
entities.label: bf ex6

entities.description:
Define s² as the MSD multiplied by the reciprocal factor n/(n−1). The divisor is valid for n > 1.
Move this fixed multiplier outside E, substitute the established expectation of MSDₙ, and cancel the two reciprocal factors.
The result is E[s²] = σ². The proof concerns variance, not automatic unbiasedness of its square root.
entities.label: bf ex7

Use c = 1/n in Var(cY) = c² Var(Y). The coefficient becomes 1/n², not 1/n.

entities.description:
Independence is used here, unlike in the expectation-linearity step.
The finite-sum variance-covariance identity has no cross covariance terms for independent observations.
Correlated observations would require those extra terms and can change the variance of the mean.

The finite sum of these n variances is nσ². Multiplication by 1/n² leaves σ²/n.

entities.description: The coefficients of the shared squared shift are −2 and +1, leaving −1. The left side is the defining MSD about the fitted sample mean. The result is exact for every sample. It does not by itself prove the estimator's average bias.

entities.description: After determining E[X̄], define the variance of that random mean by its expected squared deviation from E[X̄]. Finite second moments make this definition applicable.

entities.description: The preceding expectation calculation established E[X̄] = μ under common expectations. Substitute μ in the centering term. We did not estimate or observe the unknown population mean through this symbolic calculation.

entities.description: The mean is the finite sum divided by n. Substitute that definition inside Var to evaluate the variance of the sum using the previously introduced rules. The preceding centered-square expression explains why this variance is the expected squared mean error.

Independent, identically distributed finite-variance observations are sufficient, but the weaker common-moment and zero-covariance conditions already prove this result.

entities.description: The course roadmap groups the main lecture topics into a progression from statistical foundations to multivariate analysis and machine learning.
entities.label: def chemometrics course roadmap

entities.description: The opening scene frames Chemometrics and Applied Statistics as the connection between analytical measurements, quantitative reasoning and defensible interpretation.
entities.label: def chemometrics course title

entities.description: Chemometrics applies statistical methods to chemical data to extract meaningful information and to support the design and interpretation of chemical experiments.
entities.label: def chemometrics definition

entities.description: The introduction round gives three short anchors for sharing disciplinary background, prior chemometrics experience and programming experience.
entities.label: def chemometrics introduction round

entities.description: A compact lecturer profile gives only the background, teaching experience and research context that help students place this course.
entities.label: def chemometrics lecturer context

entities.description: A scientific result becomes reusable when interpretation, quantification and provenance remain explicit from the original analytical signal to the final artifact.

entities.description: Closing acknowledgment for the standardized data-processing presentation.
entities.label: def cogniflow closing

entities.description: The current ontology separates a learning domain and its concepts from processing resources and presentation affordances. The same semantic resources can therefore support reusable views without encoding a presentation-specific implementation.
entities.label: def cogniflow concept domain

entities.description: The CogniFlow core ontology is a deliberately small Meta-TBox: it defines the grammar used by concept domains rather than package, service, processing, runtime, or scientific domain concepts.
entities.label: def cogniflow core grammar

entities.description: A typical analytical workflow moves from instrument analysis through measured data and an open format to reusable results.
entities.label: def cogniflow coupling problem

entities.description: CogniFlow models data processing around a reusable ProcessingUnit with explicit ports. A ProcessingUnit can be specialized as an atomic ProcessingStep or a composite ProcessingPipeline; concrete scientific operations such as peak integration are specifications of that model.
entities.label: def cogniflow domain specifications

entities.description: CogniFlow treats the processing context itself as digital scientific information that can be understood by humans and machines.
entities.label: def cogniflow explicit processing context

entities.description: CogniFlow defines the rules for how functionality is described and exposed. Conforming modules combine implementation logic with machine-readable semantics and publish their capabilities through the common service boundary.
entities.label: def cogniflow extension system

entities.description: FAIR data are well-described digital objects that can be found, accessed under clear conditions, interpreted across systems and reused with sufficient context.
entities.label: def cogniflow fair data intro

entities.description: Open formats and rich metadata can make data FAIR while the processing that transforms them into a scientific result remains insufficiently described.
entities.label: def cogniflow fair processing gap

entities.description: A modern analytical laboratory combines complementary separation, mass-spectrometric, spectroscopic and electrochemical instruments.
entities.label: def cogniflow laboratory diversity

entities.description: The same semantics-first pattern can describe presentation elements: an InfoBox combines explicit text with a reusable Theme, while a concrete specification selects the actual message and visual theme.
entities.label: def cogniflow presentation specifications

entities.description: A scientific result depends on a processing history that is often much less visible than the raw data and the result themselves.
entities.label: def cogniflow processing black box

entities.description: A ProcessingPipeline composes reusable ProcessingSteps by connecting semantically compatible output and input Ports. Each step exposes the same explicit interface pattern: Input, Parameter, and Output.
entities.label: def cogniflow processing pipeline

entities.description: A reusable scientific result keeps its input, processing identity and derivation history attached to the result itself.
entities.label: def cogniflow provenance travels with data

entities.description: The same semantic resource can become RDF, a table or a chart without copying or redefining the underlying observations.
entities.label: def cogniflow same semantics different views

entities.description: CogniFlow is organized as a small core ontology surrounded by modular concept domains and concrete specification or implementation modules.
entities.label: def cogniflow semantic core

entities.description: CogniFlow separates semantic responsibility into three layers: the core provides the meta-grammar, concept domains define reusable vocabulary with that grammar, and specifications use that vocabulary to describe concrete concepts.
entities.label: def cogniflow semantic hierarchy

entities.description: Semantics makes relationships explicit by expressing statements as subject-predicate-object triples. Multiple triples that share entities naturally connect into a knowledge graph.
entities.label: def cogniflow semantic triples

entities.description: CogniFlow makes scientific meaning machine-readable so data, services and views can share one semantic contract.
entities.label: def cogniflow semantics as source

entities.description: CogniFlow describes what a processing capability means and why it exists before choosing how that capability is implemented.
entities.label: def cogniflow semantics first

entities.description: CogniFlow keeps one stable MCP-facing interface while specialized providers can evolve, move or be replaced independently.
entities.label: def cogniflow service architecture

entities.description: Consumers call Cogniflow services by capability and semantic constraints through the MCP gateway. The Semantic Authority resolves a matching ServiceOperation through Fuseki, validates the declared interface, invokes the matched executor, and returns a standardized service result. Consumer code does not import the concrete provider implementation.

entities.description: Illustrative workload across core CogniFlow provider types.

entities.description: CogniFlow standardizes meaning rather than implementations: semantics define the shared model, services provide replaceable capabilities, and those capabilities compose into reusable workflows.

A Boolean value is a logical truth value, true or false. Booleans can also be treated as a special two-category domain, but their logical meaning is distinct. Numeric, categorical and Boolean entries can be collected in vectors or rectangular arrays; the preceding real-valued matrix was only one example. These are illustrative value domains, not an exhaustive or disjoint taxonomy.

entities.description:
**Meaning**

Kurtosis averages fourth powers of deviations after removing location and scale. It is **dimensionless**, not a horizontal coordinate or an interval.

**Compare three shapes**

Uniform **K ≈ 1.800**; normal-like **2.834**; right-skewed **6.662**. Excess kurtosis subtracts the normal-population benchmark 3.

In the next point plots, larger points indicate larger fourth-power contributions. The cyan band is **mean ± two divisor-n SDs**, only a visual scale guide.

**Limit:** kurtosis is not peak height, a mode count or a tail probability. A few extreme values can dominate; m₂ must be positive.
entities.label: Kurtosis: weight of extreme standardized deviations

entities.description:
**Meaning**

The arithmetic mean is the first raw moment: the balancing point of equally weighted observations. It uses the measurement unit.

**Compare three shapes**

100 synthetic values each: uniform, normal-like and strongly right-skewed. All have mean **50 a.u.**, despite different shapes.

The next 3×3 panel shows the **same series** as points, a boxplot and a histogram. A cyan line marks the mean in every subplot.

**Limit:** the mean need not be a typical observation and is sensitive to extremes. It does not reveal spread or shape.
entities.label: First moment: the mean locates the data

entities.description:
**Meaning**

Skewness standardizes the third central moment. Positive values mean stronger positive cubic contributions; negative values mean stronger negative contributions. It is **dimensionless**.

**Compare three shapes**

Uniform and normal-like: g₁ ≈ **0**. Right-skewed: g₁ ≈ **1.759**, with mean 50 above median 46.919 a.u.

The next panels mark **mean in cyan**, **median in dashed violet**. Point size shows cubic-contribution magnitude; violet/orange distinguishes negative/positive deviations. The coefficient itself is printed, not placed on the measurement axis.

**Limit:** zero skewness does not establish symmetry or a normal distribution.
entities.label: Skewness: balance of signed cubic deviations

entities.description:
**Meaning**

Centre each value on the mean, square the deviation, then average. The result has **squared measurement units** and is unchanged by an additive offset.

**Keep conventions explicit**

Descriptive variance **m₂ uses n**. Sample variance **s² uses n−1**. For our 100-reading series, m₂ = **99 a.u.²** and s² = **100 a.u.²**.

The next panels shade **mean ± √m₂**, a scale guide in a.u., not variance itself or a fixed-coverage interval.

**Limit:** identical variance can accompany very different shapes; squaring gives extremes substantial influence.
entities.label: Second central moment: variance measures squared spread

entities.description: γ₁: population skewness; g₁: descriptive sample counterpart. Both are dimensionless; no small-sample bias adjustment is applied to g₁.
entities.label: γ₁ and g₁

entities.description: m₃: average cubed deviation from the sample mean; m₂: average squared deviation, each using n. Dividing by m₂^(3/2) removes the cubed unit. g₁ is undefined if m₂ = 0.
entities.label: m₃ and m₂

entities.label: E[ ], X, μ and σ

entities.description:
**Concept**

Replace xᵢ with its deviation **xᵢ − mean(x)** before taking powers. This removes an additive offset.

- **m₁ = 0**: deviations balance algebraically.
- **m₂**: average squared deviation, divisor **n**.
- **m₃**: signed cubic deviation balance.
- **m₄**: fourth-power deviation weight.

For n > 1, sample variance s² = n m₂/(n−1). ==Do not apply the n−1 correction mechanically to every moment.== Population central moments are expectations and require existence.
entities.label: Central moments: move the origin to the sample mean

entities.description: n: sample size; i: observation index from 1 to n; Σ: sum over those indices. Division by n forms a descriptive empirical moment.
entities.label: n, i and Σ

entities.description: r: positive integer moment order (here 1–4); mᵣ: rth empirical central moment, averaging the rth powers of deviations from x̄. Its unit is the measurement unit to power r; m₁ = 0 and m₂ uses divisor n.
entities.label: r and mᵣ

entities.description: xᵢ: value of observation i; x̄: arithmetic sample mean; xᵢ − x̄: deviation from that mean, in the measurement unit.
entities.label: xᵢ and x̄

entities.description:
**Five recovery measurements: 98, 99, 100, 101, 102%**

Mean = **100%**; deviations = **−2, −1, 0, 1, 2 percentage points**.

- First: (−2−1+0+1+2)/5 = **0**.
- Second: (4+1+0+1+4)/5 = **2**.
- Third: (−8−1+0+1+8)/5 = **0**.
- Fourth: (16+1+0+1+16)/5 = **6.8**.

The sample variance is **10/4 = 2.5**, not m₂ = 2. Adding a constant changes raw moments, but leaves all these central moments unchanged. Multiplying values by c multiplies mᵣ by cʳ.
entities.label: Central moments: calculate orders 1–4

entities.description: The rth central population moment is E[(X−μ)^r] about the population mean μ. The first is zero and the second is the population variance when the moments exist.

entities.description: A distribution is symmetric about a center c when X−c and c−X have the same distribution; zero third moment, when it exists, is necessary but not sufficient for symmetry.

entities.description: The right-continuous step function giving the fraction of observed values less than or equal to each threshold x, with equal observation weights.

entities.description: For a finite observed sample, mr=(1/n)Σ(xi−xbar)^r. This is a descriptive quantity; m2 is not the Bessel-corrected sample variance.

entities.description: The second descriptive central moment m2=(1/n)Σ(xi−xbar)². Unlike the usual unbiased sample-variance estimator s², it retains denominator n; for n>1, s²=n m2/(n−1) under the usual iid finite-variance interpretation.

entities.description: Population kurtosis minus three. Under the normal model it is zero; excess kurtosis and unadjusted kurtosis are not interchangeable.

entities.description: An empirical summary of numerical observations in adjacent value intervals (bins). Counts describe occupancy; with unequal widths, density heights ensure that bar areas represent relative frequencies.

entities.description: An empirical joint-frequency summary of paired numerical observations in rectangular cells formed from bins on each measurement axis.

entities.description: The difference between adjacent numeric bin edges. Width and origin influence the displayed aggregation and must not be confused with sample size or measurement resolution.
entities.label: l4 def histogram bin width

entities.description: The sample count in a bin divided by the total count and that bin width. Its area equals the bin relative frequency; its unit is inverse to the measurement unit.
entities.label: l4 def histogram density

entities.description: The upper quartile minus the lower quartile, using one consistent quantile convention. The linked expression defines the descriptive sample IQR using linearly interpolated quantiles, whereas Tukey boxplot hinges may differ.
entities.label: l4 def interquartile range

entities.description: The fourth standardized central population moment β2=μ4/σ⁴, defined for nonzero variance and finite fourth moment; it is sensitive to extreme deviations and is not simply peak height.
entities.label: l4 def kurtosis

entities.description: The median of the absolute differences between observations and their sample median; the raw statistic is not automatically scaled to estimate standard deviation.
entities.label: l4 def median absolute deviation

entities.description: The selected normalization and any sample-size adjustment for moment-based shape coefficients. Unadjusted sample skewness and kurtosis differ from some adjusted conventions, which must not be conflated.
entities.label: l4 def moment estimation convention

entities.description: The rth absolute population moment E[|X|^r] must be finite for the usual finite rth raw and central moments to be well-defined. Skewness requires a finite third moment and kurtosis a finite fourth moment with nonzero variance.
entities.label: l4 def moment existence

entities.description: The raw MAD multiplied by approximately 1.4826, the reciprocal of the standard normal 0.75-quantile; this is asymptotically normal-consistent, not generally finite-sample unbiased.
entities.label: l4 def normal scaled mad

entities.description: The value at a specified rank after ordering n observed real values nondecreasingly; ties are retained and rank starts at one.
entities.label: l4 def order statistic

entities.description: For the conventional 1.5×IQR rule, lower and upper reference limits around the chosen hinges or quartiles. The underlying convention must be declared.
entities.label: l4 def outlier fence

entities.description: The kth percentile is a quantile corresponding to probability p=k/100; its sample computation depends on the selected method.
entities.label: l4 def percentile

entities.description: For 0<p<1, the generalized inverse of a population cumulative distribution function F: the smallest threshold where F reaches at least p.
entities.label: l4 def population quantile

entities.description: An observation beyond a declared diagnostic fence. A flag is not evidence by itself that the value is erroneous or should be deleted.
entities.label: l4 def potential outlier

entities.description: A specified rule for turning sorted observations and a probability p into a sample quantile. Different conventions can return different results for the same sample.
entities.label: l4 def quantile estimation method

entities.description: The first, second and third quartiles correspond to p=0.25, 0.50 and 0.75; computed sample quartiles require the same explicitly chosen quantile convention.
entities.label: l4 def quartile

entities.description: The rth raw population moment is E[X^r] if the corresponding absolute moment is finite; for r=1 it is the expected value.
entities.label: l4 def raw moment

entities.description: A descriptive measure or estimator with limited sensitivity to some forms of contamination, relative to a specified perturbation criterion. Robust does not mean unaffected by every outlier.
entities.label: l4 def robust statistic

entities.description: A function of the observed sample that summarizes those observations. Its descriptive definition alone does not make it an unbiased estimator of a population parameter.
entities.label: l4 def sample descriptor

entities.description: For the declared unadjusted descriptive convention, g2=m4/m2²−3 with m2>0. Software bias corrections may instead report another estimator.
entities.label: l4 def sample excess kurtosis

entities.description: A value calculated from observed data at probability p using a declared quantile method; it can describe the sample or estimate a population quantile under sampling assumptions.
entities.label: l4 def sample quantile

entities.description: R quantile type 1 is the inverse empirical CDF for 0<p≤1, returning an observed order statistic; by endpoint convention p=0 returns the minimum.
entities.label: l4 def sample quantile type 1

entities.description: The default R sample quantile uses linear interpolation: for n>1, interpolate at knots (k−1)/(n−1); at p=1 return the maximum and for n=1 return the sole value for every p in [0,1].
entities.label: l4 def sample quantile type 7

entities.description: For a nonempty finite sample, range is maximum minus minimum, in the original measurement unit. It describes only the extrema.
entities.label: l4 def sample range

entities.description: For the declared unadjusted Fisher–Pearson convention, g1=m3/m2^(3/2), requiring m2>0. Bias-adjusted sample skewness is a different convention.
entities.label: l4 def sample skewness

entities.description: The third standardized central population moment γ1=μ3/σ³. Its sign describes the direction of moment-based asymmetry, but zero skewness alone does not prove symmetry.
entities.label: l4 def skewness

entities.description: The rth central population moment divided by σ^r, requiring σ>0 and the relevant finite moment; for r=3 and r=4 it yields skewness and non-excess kurtosis.
entities.label: l4 def standardized central moment

entities.description: A sample-dependent rule intended to infer a specified population parameter under an explicit sampling model; target, assumptions and finite-sample properties must be stated separately.
entities.label: l4 def statistical estimator

entities.description: A fixed characteristic of a specified population distribution, generally unknown when only a sample is observed. It is not the realized value of a sample statistic.
entities.label: l4 def statistical parameter

entities.description: The sample quantile calculated at probability p=0.75; its numeric value requires a specified quantile convention.
entities.label: l4 def third quartile

entities.description: A lower or upper hinge in Tukey's five-number summary. R boxplot.stats uses hinges that may differ from linearly interpolated quartiles for even sample sizes.

entities.description:
**Empirical cumulative distribution function**

For each x, count every observation with xᵢ ≤ x and divide by n. The indicator in the formula is **1 when the condition holds, otherwise 0**.

- Sort the data, retaining identities and ties.
- At each observed value, add its multiplicity/n.
- Hold the fraction constant until the next value.

==No bins, no fitted population model.== Below the minimum the ECDF is 0; at and above the maximum it is 1. It includes the jump at x: **right-continuity**.
entities.label: ECDF: one cumulative count for every threshold

entities.description:
**Scenario: compare response distributions**

Focus on the uniform and normal-like series, each n = 100. Compare the curves below and above 50 a.u.

**Interpretation**

Their curves cross: one can include a larger fraction at a low threshold and a smaller fraction at a higher threshold. ==No single mean or universal ranking answers every threshold question.==

A higher ECDF at x means **more values ≤ x**, not larger measurement values. This descriptive comparison is not a significance test or proof that one analytical method is better.
entities.label: Crossing curves: which series is higher depends on x

entities.description: Fₙ(x): unitless sample fraction at or below threshold x. The threshold x has the measurement unit.
entities.label: Fₙ(x) and x

entities.description: The value at a jump includes observations exactly at the threshold.
entities.label: The ECDF records those counts.

entities.description: Indicator: 1 when xᵢ ≤ x, otherwise 0. Equality is included: tied values enter together. Dividing the count by n gives the fraction.
entities.label: 1{xᵢ ≤ x}

entities.description:
**Scenario: the same 50 river samples**

Ask for the smallest observed x with Fₙ(x) ≥ **.25**. It is observation ceil(50 × .25) = **rank 13**, hence **6.5 mg/L**.

**Interpretation**

The generalized inverse selects an observed value. Linear interpolation instead uses h = 1 + 49 × .25 = **13.25**, between 6.5 and 7: **6.625 mg/L**.

==Both conventions are explicit, but they are not identical.== At p = 0, software conventions need separate care; the generalized inverse here is defined for 0 < p ≤ 1.
entities.label: Read backwards: inverse ECDF versus linear interpolation

entities.description:
**Same data, different histograms**

Bin width and origin change the picture, not the data. We want an empirical distribution view **without those choices**.

- **Parameter-free counting:** no bins, bandwidth or assumed distribution family.
- **Cumulative:** at each value, report the fraction **at or below it**.
- **Objective for the same data:** no subjective bin selection; sampling bias and measurement limits remain.

==The ECDF accumulates frequencies. It is not a density curve.==
entities.label: A bin-free view of the frequency distribution?

entities.description:
**Scenario**

50 constructed river concentrations: 0.5, 1.0, …, 25.0 mg/L. Not environmental evidence.

**Interpretation**

At **12.3 mg/L**, 24 observations are included: **24/50 = 48%**. There are no observations between 12 and 12.5, so this segment is flat.

At 12.5: **25/50 = 50%**. For an interval (a,b], subtract Fₙ(a) from Fₙ(b). This is an observed sample fraction, not an estimate with guaranteed precision or a regulatory conclusion.
entities.label: Answer the river question exactly

entities.description: Read horizontally from a threshold to its included cumulative fraction. Each single observation adds 1/50.
entities.label: Exact threshold fractions for 50 samples

entities.description: xᵢ: observed value i; n: sample size; i: index 1 to n; Σ: sum over every observation, including ties.
entities.label: xᵢ, n, i and Σ

entities.description:
**Scenario: four synthetic detector series**

100 observations each; all have mean **50**, sample SD **10 a.u.**

**Interpretation**

- **Uniform:** nearly steady rise across its range.
- **Normal-like:** faster rise near the centre, slower in the tails.
- **Right-skewed:** rapid early rise, then a long upper tail.
- **Bimodal:** two rising regions separated by a plateau.

Steep regions mean many observations in a short interval; a plateau means none in that interval. An ECDF is not a density curve.
entities.label: Different shapes, identical mean and SD

entities.description: 100 observations per series. Compare threshold counts; the four curves are not fitted models.
entities.label: Four shapes as cumulative fractions

entities.description: At x = 4 mg/L, the two tied values enter together: Fₙ(4) = 3/7.

entities.description:
**Seven-value hand calculation**

Sorted synthetic concentrations: **2, 4, 4, 5, 5, 6, 7 mg/L**.

- At x = 3.9: 1 value included → **1/7**.
- At x = 4: both tied 4s enter → **3/7**.
- At x = 4.1: no new value → still **3/7**.

The jump at 4 is **2/7**, not 1/7. Filled endpoints are included; open endpoints are left limits. The vertical connector is not a set of intermediate function values.
entities.label: Calculate an ECDF: include every tie

**Scenario: same mean and SD, four response shapes**

- Uniform: **1.800 / −1.200**.

entities.description:
**Concept**

A moment averages a power. The first empirical raw moment averages x itself: **a₁ = mean(x)**. Raw means measured from the chosen zero, not from the sample mean.

**Calculation**

For 98, 99, 100, 101, 102% recovery: sum = 500%, n = 5, so **a₁ = 100%**. Units are the original measurement units.

The population counterpart is E[X], when it exists. Our finite-sample descriptors use **1/n**, not an automatic bias correction.
entities.label: First raw moment: average level relative to zero

entities.description:
**Scenario: two response groups**

100 synthetic detector readings from two narrow groups near 40 and 60 a.u.

**Interpretation**

Their first raw moment is still **50 a.u.**, just as in the normal-like series. But almost no readings are near that value.

==Average level is not necessarily a typical observation.== The first moment does not encode modes, spread or the mechanism behind the two groups.
entities.label: First moment, limit: the mean can lie in a gap

entities.description: a₁: first empirical raw moment, equal to x̄. The subscript 1 is the moment order. Raw moments take powers about the chosen zero; a₁ has the original measurement unit.
entities.label: a₁

entities.description:
**Scenario: repeated control readings**

100 synthetic normal-like responses. **a₁ = 50 a.u.** summarizes their average level.

**Strength**

Useful for tracking a level or mean bias against a reference. Adding a calibration offset of **+5 a.u.** to every reading changes a₁ to **55 a.u.**, exactly as expected.

**Limit**

This says nothing about repeatability by itself. One extreme value also shifts the mean: it is not a robust centre.
entities.label: First moment, strength: track the control level

entities.description:
**Concept and calculation**

Square each reading, then average. Positive and negative readings both contribute positively. The result has **squared units**.

For 98, 99, 100, 101, 102% recovery, squared values sum to **50,010**: **a₂ = 10,002 %²**.

Useful when squared signal magnitude matters, for example a mean-square signal relative to a defined zero. Its square root is the root-mean-square value. ==a₂ is not the variance.==
entities.label: Second raw moment: average squared magnitude

entities.description:
**Scenario: change only the calibration origin**

Add 100 a.u. to the same 100 readings. Mean becomes **150**, while m₂ remains **99 a.u.²**.

**Calculation**

a₂ becomes 150² + 99 = **22,599 a.u.²**, despite unchanged spread. The diagram shows the original readings.

==Do not compare raw second moments as pure repeatability measures.== Also, the uniform and bimodal series share a₁ = 50 and a₂ = 2,599: two moments still do not identify shape.
entities.label: Second moment, limit: offsets dominate

entities.description: a₂: second empirical raw moment, the average of xᵢ². m₂: second empirical central moment, the average of (xᵢ − x̄)² with divisor n. Both have squared measurement units; m₂ is not the n−1 sample variance.
entities.label: a₂ and m₂

entities.description:
**Scenario: 100 control responses**

Mean **50 a.u.**, sample SD **10 a.u.** The divisor-n central second moment is **99 a.u.²**.

**Calculation**

a₂ = 50² + 99 = **2,599 a.u.²**; RMS ≈ **50.980 a.u.**

**Interpretation**

The mean-square signal combines average level and variation. It is useful only if both are relevant to the question and zero has a meaningful definition.
entities.label: Second moment, strength: a mean-square summary

entities.description:
**Concept and calculation**

Cube each value and average. Cubing retains the sign and magnifies large magnitudes. Units are **measurement units cubed**.

For 98, 99, 100, 101, 102% recovery, **a₃ = 1,000,600 %³**. This symmetric sample has a large positive raw third moment simply because its centre is far above zero.

==A raw third moment is not skewness.== It mixes level, spread and signed deviations.
entities.label: Third raw moment: signed cubes about zero

entities.description:
**Scenario: the symmetric 100-reading control**

On its original response scale, **a₃ = 139,850 a.u.³**, even though the signed central third moment is zero.

**Why?**

50³ + 3 × 50 × 99 + 0 = **139,850**. Translation changes raw moments. Large observations dominate cubes, so even central third moments can be unstable in small samples.

==Separate the origin from the shape question.== Zero third moment alone does not establish symmetry.
entities.label: Third moment, limit: positive cubes do not prove skew

entities.description: a₃: third empirical raw moment, average xᵢ³. m₂: average squared deviation (xᵢ − x̄)²; m₃: average cubed deviation (xᵢ − x̄)³. All averages use n. a₃ and m₃ have cubed units; m₂ has squared units.
entities.label: a₃, m₂ and m₃

entities.description:
**Scenario: use a scientifically meaningful zero**

For 100 synthetic normal-like responses, define residuals as response **minus the reference 50 a.u.** The positive and negative cubes cancel: residual a₃ ≈ **0**.

**Interpretation**

Signed cubes reveal imbalance in large deviations when the origin is justified. For the right-skewed series with the same mean and SD, residual a₃ ≈ **1,733.015 a.u.³**.

The diagram shows that right-skewed series on its original response scale. The sign summarizes imbalance, not its analytical cause.
entities.label: Third moment, strength: probe signed residual contributions

entities.description:
**Concept and calculation**

Raise every reading to the fourth power and average. Contributions are nonnegative and large magnitudes receive very high weight. Units are **measurement units to the fourth power**.

For 98, 99, 100, 101, 102% recovery, **a₄ = 100,120,006.8 %⁴**.

Useful in mathematical models involving fourth powers or for probing extreme residual contributions relative to a justified zero. ==It is not kurtosis and is not a pure tail descriptor on an arbitrary response scale.==
entities.label: Fourth raw moment: amplify large magnitudes

entities.description:
**Scenario: a reference-centred residual**

Changing a residual from **2 to 10 a.u.** multiplies its fourth-power contribution from **16 to 10,000 a.u.⁴**: a factor of **625**.

**Limit**

This sensitivity can flag scientifically important extremes, but also magnifies contamination and sampling variability. Check the actual observations and their provenance.

The right-skewed 100-reading example is shown. A finite sample always has finite moments; this does not prove that the corresponding population moments exist.
entities.label: Fourth moment, limit: one deviation can dominate

entities.description: a₄: fourth empirical raw moment, average xᵢ⁴. m₂, m₃ and m₄: averages of (xᵢ − x̄)², (xᵢ − x̄)³ and (xᵢ − x̄)⁴, respectively, each with divisor n. Their units follow the power; a₄ and m₄ have fourth-power units.
entities.label: a₄, m₂, m₃ and m₄

entities.description:
**Scenario: compare residuals about 50 a.u.**

All four constructed detector series have n = 100 and m₂ = **99 a.u.²**. Their residual fourth moments differ:

- Normal-like: **27,777.61 a.u.⁴**.
- Right-skewed: **65,297.53 a.u.⁴**.
- Uniform: **17,639.45 a.u.⁴**.
- Two clusters: **10,918.86 a.u.⁴**.

**Interpretation:** fourth powers discriminate extreme-deviation weight that the first two moments miss. They do not reconstruct the full distribution.
entities.label: Fourth moment, strength: distinguish extreme residual weight

entities.description: Both series have median=5, linearly interpolated Q1=4, Q3=5.5, IQR=1.5 and raw MAD=1 mg/L. Reference m2≈2.20408163 (mg/L)^2; extreme-series m2=82 (mg/L)^2. Robust summaries do not by themselves establish that 30 mg/L is an error.

entities.description:
**Scenario: 100 right-skewed detector responses**

With m₂ = **99**, m₃ ≈ **1,733.015**, descriptive g₁ ≈ **1.759**.

**Strength:** positive g₁ summarizes the stronger upper-deviation contribution, independent of the measurement unit and additive origin.

**Limit:** it neither proves contamination nor gives an exact tail probability. A few observations can dominate. The uniform, normal-like and bimodal examples all have g₁ ≈ 0 despite different shapes.
entities.label: Skewness: a signed shape summary, not a diagnosis

entities.description:
**Exact 50-residual counterexample**

5 residuals equal −3, 25 equal −1, and 20 equal +2 a.u. Mean = (−15−25+40)/50 = **0**.

**Calculate**

m₃ = [5(−27)+25(−1)+20(8)]/50 = **0**; m₂ = **3**; therefore g₁ = **0**.

**But the sample is asymmetric:** −3 has no matching +3 group; +2 has no matching −2 group. Signed cubes cancel without mirror symmetry. ==Inspect the distribution, not just the coefficient.==
entities.label: Zero skewness does not imply symmetry

entities.description:
**Concept and calculation**

For m₂ > 0, standardize deviations by √m₂ and average their powers. Orders 1 and 2 become **0 and 1**.

Order 3 is descriptive sample skewness **g₁ = m₃/m₂^(3/2)**. Order 4 is descriptive kurtosis **K = m₄/m₂²**; excess kurtosis is **K−3**. The normal population benchmark is K = 3, not a promise for every normal sample.

For the five recoveries: **g₁ = 0**, **K = 6.8/4 = 1.7**, excess **−1.3**.

==Undefined if m₂ = 0.== These divisor-n descriptive measures are not the bias-adjusted estimators returned by every software package.
entities.label: Standardized moments: remove the unit and scale

Each bin contains **2/8 = 25%** of the observations. Density height = count / (n × width).

- For linear interpolation, h = 1 + (n−1)p. Here n = 8.

entities.description:
The individual residual is dᵢ = Xᵢ − X̄. The common shift is Δ = X̄ − μ. Their sum gives Xᵢ − μ.
Square each side, then use the binomial identity with a = dᵢ and b = Δ.
Squaring an equality gives a consequence; sign information would be needed to reverse squaring in general.
entities.label: md bessel explanation 1

entities.description:
Sum the observation-wise equality from i = 1 to n.
Distribute the sum over all three terms. In the general rule use aᵢ = dᵢ², bᵢ = dᵢ, c = 2Δ and q = Δ².
The coefficient 2Δ is common to every observation, so it moves outside the cross-term sum. Keep the last sum explicit for now.
entities.label: md bessel explanation 2

entities.description:
These residuals were formed about their own sample arithmetic mean. Their sum is exactly zero.
Substituting Σdᵢ = 0 makes the entire cross term 2ΔΣdᵢ equal to zero.
The individual residuals and their squared sum are not zero. Only the signed residual sum vanishes.
entities.label: md bessel explanation 3

entities.description:
Within one sample, Δ = X̄ − μ does not depend on the observation index i. Its square is therefore also index-independent.
Use c = Δ² in the rule for summing a constant: the same value is added n times.
Δ is still random across repeated samples. Being constant with respect to i does not make it fixed across samples.
entities.label: md bessel explanation 4

entities.description:
Now pass from a within-sample identity to a statement about repeated sampling.
Take expectations on both sides and use linearity on the residual-square sum plus the shared-shift term.
Finite variance makes the required expectations finite. Independence is needed for later sample-mean moments, not for linearity itself.
entities.label: md bessel explanation 5

entities.description:
About the fixed population mean, each observation has expected squared deviation σ². The finite sum therefore has expectation nσ².
Use the separately established auxiliary result E[nΔ²] = σ² for the shared-shift term.
These substitutions rely on the sampling assumptions and the preceding auxiliary result, not on algebra alone.
entities.label: md bessel explanation 6

entities.description:
In the general rearrangement use a = nσ², b = E[Σdᵢ²] and c = σ².
Subtract σ² from both sides. The difference nσ² − σ² factors as (n−1)σ².
This step is algebraic once the preceding statistical moment results have been established.
entities.label: md bessel explanation 7

entities.description:
The expected residual sum of squares is (n−1)σ². Divide the statistic by the fixed positive count n−1.
Use c = 1/(n−1) in linearity of expectation, then define that normalized statistic as s². Its expectation is σ².
In contrast, dividing by n gives the descriptive MSD, whose expectation is (n−1)σ²/n. This does not make descriptive MSD erroneous. Residual degrees of freedom are a separate constraint argument; the square root s is not automatically unbiased.
entities.label: md bessel explanation 8

entities.description: Xᵢ: random observation i; X̄: sample mean; μ: population mean; dᵢ = Xᵢ − X̄; Δ = X̄ − μ. Lowercase xᵢ, x̄ are realized values.

entities.description: n > 1: count; i: index; Σ: sum from 1 to n. E: expectation; Var: variance; σ²: population variance; s²: sample variance.

entities.description: a, b, c, q: scalar placeholders; aᵢ, bᵢ: indexed terms. U, V, Y: random quantities. A constant moved outside Σ or E is fixed for that operation.
entities.label: General rule placeholders

entities.description:
The individual residual dᵢ measures Xᵢ from its sample mean X̄. The shared shift Δ measures that mean from μ.
Substitute both definitions into dᵢ + Δ. The terms −X̄ and +X̄ cancel, leaving Xᵢ − μ. In the general identity, a = Xᵢ, b = X̄, c = μ.
This is an algebraic consequence of the definitions, with no normality or independence assumption. Δ is common to the indices within a sample, but can vary across samples.
entities.label: md centers explanation
Substitute dᵢ and Δ; cancel X̄

entities.description:
For iid observations with finite variance, the sample mean has expectation μ and variance σ²/n. These are the required auxiliary moment results, not a new topic about confidence intervals.
Insert Y = X̄ into the variance definition. Because E(X̄) = μ, the expected squared shift from μ equals Var(X̄).
Uppercase X̄ denotes the random sample mean; lowercase x̄ denotes a realized value.
entities.label: md shift explanation 1

entities.description:
Set Y = Δ² and c = n in the expectation-factor rule. The sample size is fixed across repetitions.
Multiply the established expectation σ²/n by n; the factors n cancel.
Do not pull the random quantity Δ outside expectation. Only the fixed coefficient n is moved.
entities.label: md shift explanation 2

entities.description:
For each observation, dᵢ = xᵢ − x̄.
Add these equalities for i = 1 through n. The result sums the left-hand residuals and the right-hand deviations.
This implication needs no probability assumption. It does not say that one summed equation can recover all individual observations.

entities.description:
Use aᵢ = xᵢ and c = x̄ in the general rule.
Distribute the sum over subtraction. Within this observed sample, the same fitted mean is subtracted at every index. Its sum is n times x̄.
The fitted mean may change between samples, but not between indices within one sample.
entities.label: md zero explanation 2

entities.description:
The arithmetic mean is the sum of the observations divided by their count. Thus n times x̄ is exactly that same sum.
Substitute this equality into the difference of sums. A quantity minus itself is zero.
This is an exact property of the arithmetic mean, not merely a statement that residuals average to zero across repeated samples.
entities.label: md zero explanation 3

entities.description: A calibration uses standards at 0, 1, 2, 5 and 10 mg/L. Within this calibration experiment, is analyte concentration a variable or a constant?
entities.label: classify calibration concentration as variable or constant

entities.description: Every absorbance measurement in one experiment is recorded at 540 nm. Within this experiment, is wavelength a variable or a constant?
entities.label: classify fixed wavelength as variable or constant

entities.description: For each environmental sample, temperature is recorded but not controlled and the recorded values differ between samples. Within this dataset, is temperature a variable or a constant?
entities.label: classify recorded temperature as variable or constant

entities.description: You draw a frequency chart of deliberately assigned calibration concentrations. What does the chart represent?
entities.label: check empirical versus probability distribution
No — values can be assigned without a stochastic model

That measurement uncertainty equals the observed spread

entities.description: Repeated absorbance measurements vary and are modeled as outcomes of random measurement variation. Which option is the most specific description?
entities.label: quiz repeated absorbance role

entities.description: The calibration concentrations 0, 1, 2, 5 and 10 mg/L are deliberately chosen by us. What is their most specific role here?
entities.label: quiz assigned concentration role

entities.description: Every absorbance measurement is made at 540 nm. What is the wavelength's role in this experiment?
entities.label: quiz fixed wavelength role

entities.description: Several measured absorbance values differ. What can we conclude immediately from the data alone?
entities.label: check variability versus randomness and uncertainty

entities.description: A calibration uses deliberately selected concentrations of 0, 2, 4, 6 and 8 mg/L. Does the fact that concentration takes different values make it a random variable in this experiment?
entities.label: check assigned variable versus random variable

entities.description: Two analytical methods can give a similar mean result, but differ strongly in precision.
entities.label: Same Mean, Different Analytical Quality

entities.description: Precision is essential for analytical reliability, but method suitability also depends on trueness, measurement conditions, and performance requirements.
entities.label: qc precision takeaway

entities.description: The assigned control-sample target is 10 mg/L. Both illustrative arithmetic means equal this target.
entities.label: Assigned target and shared illustrative mean

entities.description: No R knowledge is required here. Press Run: each execution returns one new simulated value from a simple random-variable model.
entities.label: random draw r intro

entities.description: A relation such as X = θ + ε is an additive measurement model, not a definition of a random variable. It is appropriate only when a stable quantity θ and an additive random error term ε are justified; measurement noise must not be identified with measurement uncertainty.
entities.label: random measurement model interpretation

entities.description: The corrected sample variance statistic across hypothetical samples; lowercase s² is its realized value.
entities.label: random sample variance symbol

entities.description: Probability distributions belong to random-variable models, not to variables in general. A value range or domain is not a probability distribution. We return to distributions later.
entities.label: random variable distribution note

entities.description: A random variable is not one observed result. A die result or a measurement value is a realization of a random variable under the stated probabilistic model.
entities.label: random variable realization interpretation

entities.description: The coefficient of variation is a dimensionless ratio of a standard deviation to a nonzero mean. Cross-scale comparisons are meaningful only for ratio-scale quantities with a meaningful zero; the statistic becomes unstable when the mean is close to zero.
entities.label: relative standard deviation scope interpretation

entities.description: An integrable random quantity in an expectation identity.
entities.label: rule U symbol

entities.description: A second integrable random quantity.
entities.label: rule V symbol

entities.description: A random quantity with the moments required by the stated identity.
entities.label: rule Y symbol

entities.description: A placeholder quantity or indexed term in a general mathematical identity.
entities.label: rule a symbol

entities.description: Arithmetic mean of the same finite values a_i.
entities.label: rule abar symbol

entities.description: Insert the two defined differences. Adding them makes the intermediate value appear once with a minus sign and once with a plus sign, so it cancels.
entities.label: Substitute and cancel the intermediate center

entities.description: For n numerical observations, add the values and divide their sum by the positive count n.
entities.label: Arithmetic mean

entities.description: A second placeholder quantity or indexed term.
entities.label: rule b symbol

entities.description: Multiplying a+b by itself gives a², the two equal cross-products ab, and b². Squaring both sides of an equality is a valid implication, not generally a reversible operation without sign information.
entities.label: Binomial square

entities.description: A scalar placeholder; a fixed constant when pulled outside a sum or expectation.
entities.label: rule c symbol

entities.description: If every indexed quantity has expectation m and variance v, the sums of these expectations and variances are nm and nv. This is substitution followed by summing a constant. It says nothing by itself about the variance of a sum: that separate operation may need covariance terms.
entities.label: Substitute common moments in a finite sum

entities.description: Covariance of two random quantities; it measures their joint linear variation.
entities.label: rule cov symbol

entities.description: For U and V with finite second moments, covariance is the expected product of their centered deviations. Positive covariance indicates joint movement in the same direction, negative covariance opposing movement. Independence implies zero covariance, but zero covariance does not generally imply independence.
entities.label: Covariance definition

entities.description: Take expectations of equal integrable random quantities and distribute E over addition. Independence of the two summands is not needed for linearity.
entities.label: Linearity of expectation

entities.description: For integrable random quantities U and V, expectation distributes over their sum. A fixed coefficient c may be taken outside E. Independence is not needed for this rule.
entities.label: Linearity with a fixed multiplier

entities.description: A constant has the same value on every repetition. Its probability-weighted theoretical average is therefore that value. This is not a statement about a random observation that happens to be observed once.
entities.label: Expected value of a constant

entities.description: If integrable random quantities agree with probability one, their expectations agree. Applying E does not require independence. An equality between expectations alone does not recover equality of the random quantities, so the displayed direction is an implication.
entities.label: Expectation preserves equality

entities.description: A constant fixed across repeated samples multiplies the expectation. A random offset such as Δ must not itself be pulled outside E; the fixed count n may be.
entities.label: Factor a fixed constant out of expectation

entities.description: The sample count is fixed and positive. Move 1/n outside expectation and distribute expectation over the finite sum. This needs finite expectations, not independence. It applies to observations and also to squared deviations when their expectations exist.
entities.label: Expected value of a finite average

entities.description: For a fixed finite number of integrable random quantities, apply expectation addition repeatedly. E[ΣY_i] = ΣE[Y_i]. Neither independence nor identical distribution is required. This finite-sum rule alone does not justify interchanging an infinite sum and expectation.
entities.label: Expectation of a finite sum

entities.description: For an integrable random variable Y and fixed real a and b, multiplying the variable by a multiplies its expectation by a; adding b shifts the expectation by b. No independence assumption is needed because the other terms are constants.
entities.label: Expectation under scaling and translation

entities.description: Write a as na/n, subtract a/n and factor out a. The result holds for every real a and positive integer n. This is algebra, not an additional statistical assumption.
entities.label: Factor a common value

entities.description: Split the finite sum over subtraction, count c exactly n times, and substitute Σa_i = n ā. This needs the arithmetic mean of those same values and does not require probability assumptions.
entities.label: Sum distances from a fixed center

entities.description: For independent integrable quantities, the joint distribution factors and the expectation of the product is the product of the expectations. This is not linearity and is generally false for dependent quantities. The independence assumption also ensures integrability of the product under the stated finite absolute moments.
entities.label: Expectation of an independent product

entities.description: The indexed random quantity i in a finite sum.
entities.label: rule indexed Y symbol

entities.description: Subtract c from both sides and read the equality in reverse. This is an equivalent algebraic rearrangement.
entities.label: Subtract the same term

entities.description: Fixed coefficients and a random quantity.
entities.label: Affine expectation

entities.description: Two integrable random quantities.
entities.label: Expectation addition

entities.description: Finite variance and two fixed scalars.
entities.label: Affine variance

entities.description: Expectation and a fixed constant.
entities.label: Constant

entities.description: Both quantities have finite second moments.
entities.label: Variance and covariance

entities.description: A positive count of independent finite-variance quantities.
entities.label: Finite independent sum

entities.description: Independent quantities with finite second moments.
entities.label: Independent pair

entities.description: Finite variance and fixed coefficients.
entities.label: Variance transformation

entities.description: Common expectation of the indexed quantities.
entities.label: rule m symbol

entities.description: Expand each centered difference, distribute the finite sum, and use Σ(a_i−c) = n(ā−c). The two cross-term contributions combine with the last squared shift to leave one negative squared shift. The fitted mean removes a nonnegative term. This is an exact algebraic identity for each realization, not an expectation or an unbiasedness claim.
entities.label: Center squared distances at their arithmetic mean

entities.description: Multiplying the definition of the arithmetic mean by the positive count n gives the sum of the observations.
entities.label: Use the arithmetic mean

entities.description: Divide both sides by the same positive n. Subtract c from both sides to isolate the normalized b term. These are reversible algebraic operations and require no probability assumptions.
entities.label: Divide by a fixed count and rearrange

entities.description: Each observation has expected squared deviation σ² about μ. A finite sum gives nσ². The previously established sample-mean calculation gives E[nΔ²] = σ².
entities.label: Insert the established moment results

entities.description: A factor that does not depend on the index multiplies the entire sum.
entities.label: Factor a constant out of a sum

entities.description: A separate index-independent term; it need not be the square of another coefficient.
entities.label: rule q symbol

entities.description: Subtracting the fitted arithmetic mean from every observation creates one exact sum constraint. It is a deterministic identity, not a claim about expectation.
entities.label: Residuals sum to zero

entities.description: Fixed real scale factor in an affine transformation.
entities.label: rule scale symbol

entities.description: Expand E[(Y−E[Y])²] and use linearity. The middle term is −2(E[Y])² and the constant term is (E[Y])². Rearranging gives E[Y²] = Var(Y)+(E[Y])². A finite second moment is required; independence is not.
entities.label: Second moment and variance

entities.description: Fixed real additive shift in an affine transformation.
entities.label: rule shift symbol

entities.description: Insert an already established equality into the expression, then factor the common value. The statistical premises of the inserted result remain necessary; this algebra does not establish them.
entities.label: Substitute and factor the fixed count

entities.description: Equal values may replace one another in the same expression whenever the operations are defined. The mathematical justification of the substituted value must have been established first; substitution does not prove a statistical premise.
entities.label: Substitute an established equality

entities.description: First distribute the sum over a difference. The second sum repeats c exactly n times and equals nc.
entities.label: Split a sum and count the constant

entities.description: The same value is added once for each of n indices. A quantity can be random across samples and still be constant with respect to i within a given sample.
entities.label: Sum a constant

entities.description: Add the left sides and the right sides of equalities that hold at every index. This gives a consequence; the summed equality alone does not recover every individual equality.
entities.label: Sum indexed equalities

entities.description: A finite sum distributes over addition. No independence or probability assumption is needed.
entities.label: Linearity of a finite sum

entities.description: Use linearity for each of the three summands and move the index-independent coefficient c outside the middle sum. The last sum is not simplified yet.
entities.label: Distribute the sum and factor the cross term

entities.description: Common finite variance of the indexed quantities.
entities.label: rule v symbol

entities.description: For a fixed real constant c, E[c] = c, so c−E[c] = 0 on every outcome. Its expected squared centered deviation is therefore zero.
entities.label: Variance of a constant

entities.description: For two random quantities with finite second moments, expand the squared centered sum. The expected cross product is the covariance. Positive covariance increases the variance of the sum; negative covariance decreases it. Independence is not needed for this identity.
entities.label: Variance-covariance identity

entities.description: For a random variable with finite second moment, variance is the expected squared distance from its expectation.
entities.label: Variance is an expected squared deviation

entities.description: Mutual independence makes every cross covariance zero. The variance of the finite sum then equals the sum of its variances. For two variables this reduces to Var(U+V) = Var(U)+Var(V). Standard deviations are not directly additive.
entities.label: Variance of a finite independent sum

entities.description: Combine translation invariance with the squared scaling factor. For fixed a and b and finite variance, Var(aY+b) = a² Var(Y). Unlike expectation, variance does not acquire an additive b term.
entities.label: Variance under scaling and translation

entities.description: Variance squares the centered distance. Replacing Y by cY multiplies every centered distance by c and its square by c². Consequently variance is multiplied by c², not by c. The standard deviation is multiplied by the absolute value of c.
entities.label: Variance under scaling

entities.description: Adding a fixed c moves the random quantity and its expectation by the same amount. Their difference is unchanged, so the variance is unchanged. This does not hold for adding an arbitrary random quantity.
entities.label: Variance under translation

entities.description: For a finite collection with finite second moments, the variance-covariance identity includes all pairwise cross covariances. When each is zero, only the individual variances remain. Independence is sufficient for this result but pairwise zero covariance is enough.
entities.label: Variance of a pairwise uncorrelated sum

entities.description: sample standard deviation
entities.label: s symbol

entities.description: The sample arithmetic mean is a statistic computed from observed data and can be used to estimate a population expected value under an appropriate sampling model. It is not semantically identical to the expected value of a random variable.
entities.label: sample mean estimator interpretation

entities.description: The sample arithmetic mean is a statistic computed from observed data.
entities.label: sample mean estimator interpretation keypoint 1

entities.description: Under an appropriate sampling model it can estimate a population expected value, but it is not semantically identical to that expected value.
entities.label: sample mean estimator interpretation keypoint 2

entities.description: A statistical sample is a collection of observations or observational units. A concrete recorded value such as x_i is an observation or realization of a variable, not the sample itself. In analytical chemistry the word sample can also mean a physical specimen, so the statistical and chemical meanings must be distinguished from context.
entities.label: sample variable interpretation

entities.description: 3  COLUMN = ONE VARIABLE
entities.label: sample variable keypoint column

entities.description: 4  COLUMN VALUES → EMPIRICAL DISTRIBUTION
entities.label: sample variable keypoint distribution

entities.description: 1  SAMPLE = SET OF OBSERVATIONS
entities.label: sample variable keypoint observation

entities.description: 2  ROW = ONE OBSERVATION
entities.label: sample variable keypoint row

entities.description: A rectangular data table makes the Sample–Variable relationship concrete.
entities.label: sample variable principles

entities.description: Die Standardabweichung ist die nichtnegative Quadratwurzel einer Varianz. Zur konventionellen Bessel-korrigierten Schätzung der Populationsvarianz aus einer Stichprobe wird durch n − 1 geteilt; für eine vollständig betrachtete Population wird durch N geteilt. Das bedeutet nicht, dass jede rein deskriptive Standardabweichung einer Stichprobe zwingend n − 1 verwendet, und das Wurzelziehen ergibt nicht automatisch einen unverzerrten Schätzer der Populationsstandardabweichung.
entities.label: sd definition university de

entities.description: Standard deviation is the non-negative square root of a variance. For the conventional Bessel-corrected estimation of population variance from a sample, division is by n − 1; for a fully observed population, division is by N. This does not mean that every purely descriptive standard deviation of sample data must use n − 1, and taking the square root does not automatically yield an unbiased estimator of population standard deviation.
entities.label: sd definition university en

entities.description: μ is the population mean; X̄ is fitted from the same n observations Xᵢ. σ² is the population variance.
entities.label: Fit the mean

entities.description: Residuals sum to zero: Σᵢ(Xᵢ − X̄) = 0. Only n − 1 residuals are free; SS_res is their sum of squares.
entities.label: One constraint

entities.description: Var(X̄) = σ²/n. Thus the fitted-mean term contributes σ² in expectation; the full sum contributes nσ².
entities.label: Mean contribution

entities.description: Divide SS_res by n − 1: E[s²] = σ². Division by n instead gives (n − 1)σ²/n on average.
entities.label: Correct the denominator

entities.description: The total sum of squares about the population mean equals the residual sum of squares about the sample mean plus n times the squared distance between the two means. Taking expectations leaves n minus one times population variance for residuals.
entities.label: v11 formula

entities.description:
Known population: μ = 10 mg/L, σ² = 4 (mg/L)². Sample size n = 3.
Expected SS/n: 8/3 ≈ 2.667 (mg/L)².
Expected SS/(n − 1): 4 (mg/L)².
Monte Carlo averages approximate these expectations; they need not equal them.
entities.label: Bessel's Correction in a Simulation

entities.description: Squaring creates squared units; the non-negative square root restores the measurement unit. SD describes a typical scale of spread, not the mean absolute distance. The square root of an unbiased variance estimator is not automatically an unbiased SD estimator.
entities.label: From Variance to Standard Deviation

entities.description:
Series B: s² = 25 (mg/L)².
Squared deviations produce squared concentration units.
entities.label: Variance: squared spread

entities.description:
Take the non-negative root.
√25 = 5; √[(mg/L)²] = mg/L.
entities.label: Transformation: square root

entities.description:
Series B: s = 5 mg/L.
Now the spread is expressed on the concentration scale.
entities.label: SD: original measurement unit

entities.description: Read the expression as a sequence: center, square, sum, divide by residual degrees of freedom, then take the square root.
entities.label: Reading the Standard Deviation Formula

entities.description: One constraint after fitting the mean.
entities.label: n − 1: residual degrees of freedom

entities.description: Estimated from the same observations.
entities.label: x̄: sample mean

entities.description: Count the relevant sampled units; n > 1.
entities.label: n: number of observations

entities.description: Non-negative; same unit as xᵢ.
entities.label: s: sample standard deviation

entities.description: Add all n squared deviations.
entities.label: Σ: sum over observations

entities.description: One measured value; i identifies the observation.
entities.label: xᵢ: individual observation

entities.description: The visible spread now has a numerical scale: s(A) = 1 mg/L; s(B) = 5 mg/L. Both means remain 10 mg/L.
entities.label: Same Data, Different Standard Deviations

entities.description: Six minutes: calculate n, mean, SS, variance and SD for both series. Check the manual denominators against var() and sd(). Values are in mg/L; variances in (mg/L)².

entities.description:
Six minutes: calculate n, mean, SS, variance and SD for both series. Compare the manual calculations with var() and sd().
Why does var() divide by n − 1? Change one value: predict which summaries change, then run again. Concentrations and SDs are in mg/L; variances are in (mg/L)².

entities.description: T10 and T12 both show small spreads, but T12 has an observed center 2 mg/L above the reference. Small spread alone cannot establish trueness. These finite-sample centers are not known long-run expected results.

entities.label: v17 a1

entities.label: v17 b2

entities.description: Accuracy concerns closeness to a true quantity value and is related to both trueness and precision. It is not a synonym for precision or SD. A small SD can coexist with a systematic offset.

entities.description: Both observed means equal the target. A has the smaller sample SD: evidence of better repeatability here, not proof of zero bias or of long-term performance. Five results give only a limited precision estimate.

entities.description: Report which conditions were held constant and which changed. A short-term repeatability SD is not interchangeable with an intermediate-precision or between-laboratory reproducibility SD.

Same procedure, operator, instrument and location; short interval.
Example: replicate QC determinations in one session under fixed conditions.

Example: an interlaboratory study of a specified measurement procedure.

entities.label: v22 context

entities.description: Sources may interact or be correlated. Calibration can also be carried out in parallel; this illustrative sequence does not assert a mandatory timing or additive independent variances.
entities.label: Sources along the analytical workflow

entities.description: Location; heterogeneity
entities.label: Sampling

entities.label: Calibration

entities.label: Measurement

entities.description: Six minutes: evaluate the same five results per method under fixed measurement conditions.
entities.label: R Lab 2: Evaluating QC Measurements

entities.description:
Six minutes: calculate mean, variance, SD and the count within the illustrative 9.5–10.5 mg/L interval (endpoints included).
Does the smaller observed SD support better precision for A under these conditions? What can five results not establish about trueness or long-term performance? Means and SDs are in mg/L; variances are in (mg/L)².
entities.label: v23 task

entities.description: Interpret RSD only for a suitable ratio-scale quantity: ratios and an absolute zero must be meaningful, and the mean must be sufficiently separated from zero for the purpose. For positive concentrations, the RSD ratio equals CV = s/x̄.
entities.label: Relative Standard Deviation

entities.description: Relative standard deviation is the dimensionless ratio of sample standard deviation to the magnitude of the sample mean. Multiplying the ratio by one hundred gives its numerical percentage value.
entities.label: v24 formula

entities.description: The bars mean absolute value. Our concentration means are positive. A nonzero denominator alone does not guarantee a scientifically useful ratio.
entities.label: |x̄|: nonzero mean magnitude

entities.description: A ratio of 0.02 is 2%. Multiplication by 100 changes the numerical reporting scale, not the physical dimension.
entities.label: 100: report the ratio as percent

entities.description: Absolute spread in the same unit as the sample mean. The units cancel in their ratio: RSD is dimensionless.
entities.label: s: sample SD

entities.description: For these five repeats, B's relative spread is about 6.37 times A's. This compares sample dispersion under the stated conditions, not trueness or guaranteed long-term performance.
entities.label: RSD in Analytical Quality Control

entities.description: A
entities.label: v25 a1

entities.description: B
entities.label: v25 b1

entities.description: RSD expresses SD as a percentage of the concentration level rather than in mg/L.
entities.label: v25 key

entities.description: Both means are 10 mg/L: the SD and RSD rankings are identical, not independent evidence.
entities.label: v25 key2

entities.description: Compute from unrounded SDs. Display SD to three decimals and RSD to two; both SDs use n − 1 = 4.
entities.label: v25 key3

entities.description: A: about 1.58%; B: about 10.07%. Both use the sample SD with n − 1 = 4.
entities.label: Same center, different relative spread

entities.description: The mean and SD both increase tenfold, so their ratio stays constant: RSD = 2%. Equal relative spread does not mean equal absolute spread. Such comparisons still require a compatible quantity, meaningful zero and relevant measurement conditions.
entities.label: Absolute vs Relative Spread

entities.description: Illustrative summaries: identical bar heights show equal RSD, while the table shows different absolute SDs.
entities.label: Same relative spread at different levels

entities.description: Derived summaries for two illustrative levels, not individual measured observations: 100 times 0.2/10 and 100 times 2/100 both equal 2 percent.
entities.label: v26 rsd data

entities.description: Even on a concentration scale with a meaningful zero, a blank mean near zero is a poor denominator. Blank-corrected estimates may be positive or negative. Celsius temperature has a different problem: its arbitrary zero makes RSD inappropriate regardless of the denominator's size.
entities.label: When RSD Is Misleading

entities.description: Mean = 0.001 mg/L; SD = 0.020 mg/L. RSD = 2000%, driven by a tiny denominator.
entities.label: Illustrative blank

entities.description: Division by zero: RSD is undefined, not zero. Near zero it is unstable and can change drastically.
entities.label: Exactly zero mean

entities.description: Ratios require a meaningful zero. Absolute values in the denominator do not repair arbitrary scale origins.
entities.label: Check the measurement scale

entities.description: undefined
entities.label: v27 e3

entities.description: Hold absolute SD fixed at 0.020 mg/L. Only the illustrative mean changes.
entities.label: v27 k1

entities.description: At a zero mean, RSD is undefined; near zero it is unstable. Taking an absolute value does not fix this.
entities.label: v27 k2

entities.description: A huge RSD alone does not prove a poor method. For blanks, assess absolute SD and the relevant detection or decision requirements.
entities.label: v27 k3

entities.description:
Compare n = 3 and n = 30 from the same iid normal population: μ = 10 mg/L, σ = 2 mg/L.
Sample variance is unbiased: E[s²] = 4 (mg/L)². Sample SD is generally not unbiased for σ.
Monte Carlo means approximate expectations; SD percentiles describe repeated estimates, not a confidence interval for σ from one sample.
entities.label: How Much Can We Trust a Sample SD?

entities.description: Squared deviations make variance and SD sensitive to extreme values; the mean shifts too. Investigate the cause and measurement context. An unusual result may be real and must not be deleted solely because it changes the summaries.
entities.label: One Extreme Value Changes Everything

entities.description: Original

entities.description: Modified
