entities.label: v29 context

entities.description: Synthetic teaching modification of QC Method A: only its final value changes from 10.2 to 15.2 mg/L. No published observations are changed.
entities.label: v29 data

entities.description: Same unit does not mean same scale: raw MAD and IQR are not interchangeable with SD. Normal-model scaling is assumption-dependent, not a universal conversion. Robust summaries reduce sensitivity to extremes; they do not establish that an observation is erroneous.
entities.label: Robust Measures of Spread

entities.description: Sample SD: square root of SS/(n − 1), centered on the mean (11 mg/L here). Squaring makes it sensitive to the extreme result.
entities.label: SD: 2.351 mg/L

entities.description: xᵢ: an observation; median(x) = 10 mg/L; | · |: absolute distance. Take the median of these distances. In R: mad(x, constant=1).
entities.label: Raw MAD: 0.100 mg/L

entities.description: Q₃ − Q₁ = 10.1 − 9.9 mg/L using R's default type-7 quartiles. It describes the width of the central half, not a standard deviation.
entities.label: IQR: 0.200 mg/L

entities.description: Default: 1.4826 × raw MAD = 0.14826 mg/L before rounding. This large-sample normal-consistency scaling is not a small-sample unbiasedness correction.
entities.label: R mad(): 0.148 mg/L

entities.description: Seven minutes: compare a synthetic modification with the original QC measurements. Keep both datasets and document the change.
entities.label: R Lab 3: Explore the Influence of Outliers

entities.description:
Seven minutes: compare mean, median, SD, IQR and both versions of MAD before and after replacing 10.2 with 15.2 mg/L. All reported results here are in mg/L.
Which summaries react most, and why? Does stability of MAD or IQR establish that the observation is wrong? Explain why investigation must precede any exclusion.
entities.label: v31 task

entities.description: Repeated independent samples of the same size from one population would generate a distribution of sample means. This sampling distribution differs from the distribution of individual observations. Three sample means only illustrate the idea; they do not estimate that distribution reliably.
entities.label: The Spread of Observations and Means

entities.description: Nine individual values versus one mean per sample. These three synthetic means are an illustration, not a simulated sampling distribution.
entities.label: Individual results versus sample means

entities.description: So far, we have described how individual measurements vary. Now we ask how the mean itself varies between independent samples. Each illustrative sample contains n = 3 individual values and yields exactly one mean; recalculating the same data does not create a new sample.
entities.label: v32 context

entities.description: Means of the three synthetic samples: 10, 11, 9 mg/L. Three means illustrate the idea, not a well-estimated sampling distribution.
entities.label: v32 means

entities.description: Nine synthetic values in three illustrative samples; sample membership is given in the companion table.
entities.label: v32 observations
Three values → one mean (all in mg/L)

entities.description: For independent, identically distributed observations with finite variance, the true SEM is σ/√n. Replacing σ by s estimates it. Observation spread and precision of a mean estimate are different; SEM alone is not a complete measurement uncertainty.
entities.label: Standard Error of the Mean

entities.description: Estimated SD of the distribution of sample means across repeated samples. True SEM = σ/√n; the hat marks the estimate using s. Units are the same as the observations.
entities.label: Estimated SE / SEM

entities.description: The sample SD describes individual results, not the variability of sample means. Neither s nor SEM alone is a complete uncertainty budget or a measure of systematic error.
entities.label: s: individual-observation spread

entities.description: The simple formula requires independent, identically distributed observations with finite variance. Which observations actually count as independent observations in n? Count relevant independent sampling units, not automatically every injection.
entities.label: n: independent observations

entities.description: Four times as many independent observations halve SE: √(4n) = 2√n. Averaging reduces random variation in the mean; it does not change the individual-result SD σ or remove a systematic error.
entities.label: More Measurements, Smaller Standard Error

entities.description:
SE = 2/√4 = 1 mg/L.
Assumed individual-observation SD: 2 mg/L.
entities.label: n = 4

entities.description:
SE = 2/√16 = 0.5 mg/L.
Same population SD, four times as many independent data.
entities.label: n = 16

entities.description:
SE = 2/√64 = 0.25 mg/L.
Again four times the sample size, half the SE.
entities.label: n = 64

entities.description: Theoretical SE = σ/√n with assumed σ = 2 mg/L throughout. These are model calculations, not simulated measurements.
entities.label: Fourfold sample size, half the SE

entities.description: Theoretical standard errors σ/sqrt(n) for independent identically distributed observations with assumed σ = 2 mg/L. Derived summaries, not individual measured observations.
entities.label: v34 data
Hold population SD σ = 2 mg/L fixed

entities.description: The simple SEM assumes iid observations with finite variance. Label error bars explicitly: SD and SEM answer different questions; RSD describes relative spread, not the uncertainty of the estimated mean.
entities.label: SD, SE and RSD: Three Different Questions

entities.description: How much do individual results vary? SS: sum of squared deviations about x̄; n: count of observations. Sample SD uses n − 1 residual df and has the original measurement unit.
entities.label: SD: individual observations

entities.description: How much would the sample mean vary across independent repetitions? s: sample SD; n: independent observations per sample. The estimate has the original unit; it is not individual-result dispersion.
entities.label: SE: repeated sample means

entities.description: How large is SD relative to the mean? s/|x̄| is dimensionless; ×100 reports percent. |x̄| is the nonzero mean magnitude. Interpretation needs a suitable ratio scale and a mean away from zero.
entities.label: RSD: spread relative to level

entities.description: μ is fixed and unknown. The interval varies across samples but is fixed once the data are observed. For iid normal observations, n > 1 and unknown variance, 95% refers to long-run coverage of the procedure—not a 95% probability for μ in this particular interval.
entities.label: Confidence Interval for the Mean

entities.description: α is the significance level of the corresponding two-sided test and nominal noncoverage rate. Confidence level = 1 − α. For 95%, α = 0.05, split as α/2 in each tail.
entities.label: α and confidence level

entities.description: The (1 − α/2) quantile of Student's t distribution. Residual degrees of freedom: n − 1, because the mean is estimated from the same n observations.
entities.label: t critical value and df

entities.description: s: sample SD; n: independent observations. The estimated SD of sample means, in measurement units. Multiply by t to obtain the margin.
entities.label: s/√n: estimated SEM

entities.description: x̄ is the observed sample mean. Subtract/add the margin for lower/upper endpoints targeting the population mean μ, not individual observations.
entities.label: x̄ and the endpoints

entities.description: Under iid normal sampling, this interval estimates μ. It is not a specification for individual results and does not include every systematic or calibration contribution to measurement uncertainty. Calculate with unrounded values; round only for reporting.
entities.label: Confidence Interval: Worked Analytical Example

entities.description: n = 5 repeats; x̄ = 10 mg/L; sample variance s² = 0.025 (mg/L)². Its square root gives s ≈ 0.1581 mg/L.
entities.label: QC A: sample summaries

entities.description: Estimated SEM = s/√5 ≈ 0.07071 mg/L. df = 4; α = 0.05 gives t* = t(0.975,4) ≈ 2.776. The t value is dimensionless.
entities.label: SE and critical t

entities.description: Margin t* × SEM ≈ 0.1963 mg/L. Subtract/add it to x̄ = 10 mg/L. Report endpoints to three decimals; intermediate labels here are rounded approximations.
entities.label: Margin → endpoints

entities.description: QC Method A: the two-sided ninety-five percent t interval is approximately ten plus or minus 0.1963 milligrams per litre, giving endpoints 9.804 and 10.196 milligrams per litre.
entities.label: v37 formula

entities.description: Seven minutes: calculate a two-sided 95% t interval manually, then compare t.test().
entities.label: R Lab 4: Confidence Intervals

entities.description:
Seven minutes: assuming iid normal QC repeats, calculate the mean, SD, SE and qt() critical value. Compare the manual 95% interval with t.test().
The width comparison holds s fixed for hypothetical independent sample sizes. New data can also change s. Copying the same values does not create independent evidence or justify a smaller SE.
entities.label: v38 task

entities.description: Compare sites, independent samples within a site, preparations within a sample, and instrumental repeats within a preparation. A lower-level repeat does not measure every higher-level source. Independent, additive variance components require an appropriate model; nesting alone does not establish them.
entities.label: Variability Occurs at Different Levels

entities.description: Each parent may have several children. The four boxes show levels, not four independent observations.
entities.label: A nested analytical workflow

entities.description: Between-site variation
entities.label: Sampling site

entities.description: Between samples within a site
entities.label: Independent sample

entities.description: Between preparations of a sample
entities.label: Sample preparation

entities.description: Instrumental replicates within a preparation
entities.label: Instrument repeat

entities.description: Same fifteen values as in Variables. Within-site spread compares three values at one site; between-site variation compares sites, for example their means. Observed differences do not identify causes: three values per site cannot separate sampling, preparation and instrument variance without a suitable experimental design.
entities.label: Lake Sampling: Within-Site and Between-Site Variation

entities.description: Three measurement replicates per site, on one common concentration axis. Their sampling/preparation independence is not established by the plot.
entities.label: Lake analyte A: the original fifteen values

entities.description: The number of measurements is not necessarily the number of independent experimental units. An independent unit supplies separate evidence for the target question under the design and assumptions. Pseudoreplication counts dependent or nested readings as if they were such units; the label ‘replicate’ does not establish independence.
entities.label: What Counts as an Independent Replicate?

entities.description: Technical replicates: repeated readings of the same material. Capture injection/instrument variation, not preparation or field-sampling variation. Shared drift can still cause dependence.
entities.label: Three injections, one vial

entities.description: Separately prepare aliquots of one sample. Can capture preparation plus downstream measurement variation. They share the field sample and are not three independent field units.
entities.label: Three independent preparations

entities.description: Separately collect, prepare and measure samples. Can capture sampling plus downstream variation. Independent evidence for a field target depends on spatial/temporal design and shared conditions.
entities.label: Three independent field samples

entities.description: For a linear model with a full-column-rank design matrix, residual df = n − p. Here p counts independent estimated model coefficients. This is a model-rank statement, not a universal formula for every statistical procedure.
entities.label: Degrees of Freedom Beyond the Mean

entities.description: X is the linear-model design matrix. For ordinary least squares, full column rank gives p independently estimable coefficients and p residual constraints. In general, residual df = n − rank(X).
entities.label: n observations, p estimable parameters

entities.description: p = 1: one intercept/mean. Residual df = n − 1.
entities.label: Estimate one mean

entities.description: p = 2: intercept and slope. With distinct x values and full rank, residual df = n − 2.
entities.label: Fit a straight line

entities.description: Illustrative UV/Vis calibration: five standards, two fitted coefficients, three residual df. OLS fit: intercept 0.044 a.u.; slope 0.982 a.u. per mg/L; SS residual = 0.01824 a.u.²; s_res ≈ 0.07797 a.u. It measures response scatter about the fitted line, not concentration uncertainty.
entities.label: Residual Standard Deviation in Calibration

entities.description: Only the fitted model is drawn. Endpoint markers are model predictions, not observations. Observed signals appear in the table: the current line-chart contract cannot show an unconnected observation series alongside the fitted line.
entities.label: OLS model: ŷ = 0.044 + 0.982x

entities.description: Illustrative UV/Vis calibration standards; concentrations 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 mg/L.
entities.label: Observed signals

entities.description: xᵢ: standard concentration; yᵢ: observed response; ŷᵢ: predicted response. β₀: intercept; β₁: slope; εᵢ: model error. n − 2: residual df. Interpreting s_res as an error SD assumes independent zero-mean errors of common variance and a suitable linear model.
entities.label: Model and residuals
Observed y, fitted ŷ and residual (a.u.)

entities.description: Six minutes: fit a calibration line with intercept and slope and inspect its residual spread.
entities.label: R Lab 5: Residual Degrees of Freedom

entities.description:
Six minutes: use lm(), coef(), residuals() and df.residual(). Check the manual residual SD against summary(fit)$sigma.
Why do fitting an intercept and slope leave only three residual df? Explain what this signal-scale SD describes and why it is not concentration uncertainty.
entities.label: v44 task

entities.description: Discuss two QC methods using five repeats each. The inclusive interval [9.5, 10.5] mg/L is an illustrative teaching rule, not a validated routine-performance requirement. These results alone cannot establish routine suitability.
entities.label: Analytical Decision Challenge

entities.description: A
entities.label: v45 a1

entities.description: B
entities.label: v45 b1

entities.description:
Discuss in pairs: what would you report about A versus B from these five results each? Compare means, SD, RSD and counts in the inclusive illustrative interval [9.5, 10.5] mg/L.

entities.description: Precision is closeness of agreement among repeated measurement results under stated conditions. A standard deviation quantifies the spread of such results, but it must be associated with a specified measurand, procedure and measurement conditions.

entities.description: Closeness of agreement among repeated measurement results under stated conditions.

entities.description: Smaller SD means less observed spread. Precision depends on stated measurement conditions.
entities.label: Standard deviation

entities.label: Repeatability

entities.label: Intermediate precision

entities.description: Scenario: different laboratories analyze the same homogeneous QC material using a specified procedure. Their results assess between-laboratory conditions. These labels do not imply a universal ordering of SDs.
entities.label: Reproducibility

entities.label: vr28a

entities.description: A has smaller observed SD. Five repeats provide limited evidence about long-term performance.

Why Precision Alone Is Not Enough

entities.description: Closeness of the long-run mean result to a reference value. A small SD alone does not establish trueness.
entities.label: Trueness

entities.description: Long-run mean result minus the reference value. A tightly clustered set of results can still have an offset.
entities.label: Bias

entities.description: Requires relevant performance requirements and measurement conditions, not only a small observed SD.
entities.label: Method suitability
What Counts as an Independent Replicate?

entities.description: Inject one prepared vial three times. These technical replicates assess instrumental variation, not new preparation or field sampling. Shared drift may still make the readings dependent.
entities.label: Three injections, one vial

entities.description: Prepare three aliquots of one field sample separately and measure each. This captures preparation plus downstream variation. They share the field sample; independent preparation errors require justified assumptions about common batch effects. They are not three field units.
entities.label: Three independent preparations

entities.description: Collect, prepare and measure three field samples separately. These may be independent experimental units for a field question, depending on spatial and temporal design. Pseudoreplication counts nested readings as separate field units.
entities.label: Three independent field samples

entities.description: Repeating only instrument readings misses earlier sources of variation.

entities.description: E: repeated-sampling expectation; σ²: population variance; MSDₙ: residual sum of squares divided by n. Here σ² = 5 (mg/L)².
entities.label: The variance target

entities.description: Subtract E(nΔ²) = σ² from nσ². Assumptions: independent identical sampling, finite variance. Normality is not needed.

entities.description: Bias concerns expectation, not each realization. Why does fitting the mean reduce squared deviations?

entities.description: X̄: random sample mean; x̄: realized value. μ: population mean; σ²: finite population variance; n > 1: sample size.
entities.label: Random mean, fixed population

entities.description: E: expectation; Var: variance; Δ = X̄ − μ. E(Δ²) = Var(X̄). Assumptions: independent, identically distributed observations. Normality is not required.
entities.label: Expected squared shift

entities.description: Δ = X̄ − μ. Because E(X̄) = μ, E(Δ²) = Var(X̄). Multiply by fixed n. Normality is not required.
entities.label: The needed auxiliary result

entities.description: Prepared instructor demonstration: interpret the estimates, not the R programming.

entities.label: Five Samples at Every Size

entities.label: Values and sums

entities.label: One common shift

entities.description: The solid curve is the derived expectation; points are seeded Monte Carlo averages. The dashed line is the true population variance.
entities.label: Theory and Monte Carlo

entities.description: s²: sample variance; dᵢ: observation i minus its fitted mean; n > 1: count; Σ: sum over i = 1 to n.
entities.label: Sample variance

entities.label: Remove average bias

entities.label: Keep the arguments separate

entities.label: Symbols

entities.label: Square all terms

entities.label: The cross term vanishes

entities.description: Δ = X̄ − μ; μ: population mean; n: count. The shared squared shift occurs n times. Superscript 2 means square.
entities.label: The offset remains

entities.description: The same quantity can take different values for different reasons. In our UV/Vis experiment we choose concentrations. In the lake we observe them.
entities.label: why values differ intro

entities.description: Some differences are created by design. Others arise in the sampled system or measurement process. A variable's role depends on the study design.
entities.label: why values differ takeaway

entities.description: Fünf Wiederholbestimmungen einer Koffeinprobe werden mit Mittelwert und Bessel-korrigierter Stichprobenstandardabweichung ausgewertet. Die Streuung beschreibt die Präzision unter den angegebenen Wiederholbedingungen; ohne Referenzwert oder Wiederfindung wird keine Richtigkeit abgeleitet.
entities.label: caffeine determination

entities.description: In a UV/Vis calibration series, analyte concentration is deliberately changed between standards and therefore acts as the independent variable. Absorbance is the measured dependent response. The measurement wavelength is held at 540 nm and is therefore a constant within this experiment.
entities.label: UV/Vis calibration roles

entities.description: Illustrative concentrations in mg/L: samples A, B and C; nitrate and phosphate.
entities.label: worked example concentration value shapes

entities.description: A measured concentration may be modeled as a continuous random variable over the physically admissible range when the measurement model treats concentration as continuously valued.
entities.label: concentration as a continuous random variable

entities.description: For a fixed sampled volume and counting protocol, the observed number of colonies is integer-valued and can be modeled as a discrete random variable.
entities.label: colony count as a discrete random variable

entities.description: A traveler covers two equal-distance sections at 10 m/s and 2 m/s. Total distance divided by total travel time gives 10/3 m/s ≈ 3.33 m/s, equal to the harmonic mean of the two speeds.
entities.label: average speed over equal-distance sections

entities.description: Target unit: µg/L. Table A Fe is already 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 µg/L and therefore remains 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 µg/L. Table A Cu values 0.2, 0.3 and 0.4 mg/L become 200, 300 and 400 µg/L. Table B Fe values 0.0003, 0.0007 and 0.0011 mg/L become 0.3, 0.7 and 1.1 µg/L. Table B Cu values 0.15, 0.25 and 0.335 mg/L become 150, 250 and 335 µg/L.
entities.label: corrected concentration-unit harmonization example

entities.description: In a chromatographic calibration, standard concentration is deliberately varied and acts as the independent variable, while peak area is the dependent response. The nominal injection-volume setting is kept at 5 µL and is a constant within this calibration.
entities.label: chromatographic calibration roles

entities.description: Two equal successive periods have multiplicative factors 2 and 8. Their geometric mean is 4, and applying factor 4 in each period preserves the total factor: 4 × 4 = 2 × 8 = 16.
entities.label: equivalent multiplicative growth factor

entities.description: Fünf pH-Werte werden über Mittelwert, Abweichungen, Quadratsumme und Stichprobenstandardabweichung ausgewertet.
entities.label: repeated pH measurement

entities.description: For 2.1, 2.3, 2.0, 2.2 and 45.0 NTU, the arithmetic mean is 10.72 NTU and the median is 2.2 NTU. The example illustrates the greater resistance of the median to one extreme observation; which summary is scientifically preferable still depends on the question being asked.
entities.label: turbidity data with one extreme observation

entities.description: Illustrative analytical data: a concentration of 2.55 mg/L, a replicate count of 3, an impedance of 2 + 3i ohms, a sample class of lake and a passed quality check.
entities.label: worked example variable value types

entities.description: When nitrate concentrations are compared between sampling sites, sampling site can act as an independent explanatory or grouping variable and nitrate concentration as the dependent response, while the analytical protocol keeps the nominal aliquot volume at 10.0 mL as a constant. Because site is observed rather than experimentally manipulated, this role assignment alone does not establish a causal effect of site.
entities.label: environmental sampling roles

entities.description: sample arithmetic mean
entities.label: xbar symbol

entities.description: i-th observed value
entities.label: xi symbol

entities.description: Using the sample mean and the same sample-standard-deviation convention gives transformed sample values with sample mean 0 and sample standard deviation 1 when s is non-zero. Using population parameters gives population mean 0 and population standard deviation 1 when sigma is non-zero. The conventions must not be mixed silently.
entities.label: z score convention interpretation

entities.description: Ordinary mean-and-standard-deviation z-score standardization is not robust to outliers: extreme observations can affect both the centering mean and the scaling standard deviation.
entities.label: z score outlier sensitivity interpretation

blocks.text: In statistics, a variable is a characteristic or quantity that can take different values within a stated dataset, study, model or experiment. Its values may be observed, measured, assigned or controlled.

items.text: Describe experiments through individual aspects of a system.
Examine aspects separately, while stating the conditions.

blocks.text: We prepare five calibration standards with chosen concentrations and measure their absorbance. Concentration and absorbance are variables. Each row is one observation of a calibration standard and each cell contains one variable value. The plot shows the same concentration–absorbance observations graphically.

descriptions.value: Course orientation, lecturer context, learning workflow, materials and introduction activities.
Basic statistical measures, location and dispersion, distributions and statistical moments.
Hypothesis testing, t- and F-tests, distribution tests, ANOVA, multivariate similarity, clustering and component analysis.
Linear and non-linear regression, model diagnostics and machine-learning methods for prediction and classification.
Normalization, smoothing and denoising with convolution, Savitzky-Golay methods, Fourier filtering and wavelet analysis.
Measurement uncertainty, uncertainty propagation, errors and bias, outliers, bootstrap methods and classification-error concepts.
Downhill-simplex optimization and design of experiments including factorial, fractional and response-surface designs.
